newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Zinc's star in base metal complex rising.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Zinc's star in base metal complex rising.

text.p: Zinc will be a bright star in the base metal complex this year, with prices and premiums seen punching higher on robust demand and falling stocks, a senior official at Canadian miner Cominco Ltd said on Tuesday.
"People will be scrambling for zinc," Colin Blyth, managing director of Asia Pacific Cominco Metals pte Ltd, said in an interview with Reuters.

"I think there is a very good chance for a price increase further from today's level in the second half (of this year). We do see a trend higher. I could see another US$100 getting added to the price from the current level without a lot of difficulty," he said.
Zinc jumped to a 4-1/2 year high on Monday on the London Metal Exchange (LME), hitting a peak of $1,240/42 a tonne before finishing $21 up on the day at $1,239.
The forecast extension of the metal's rally in the second half of 1997 is expected to be fuelled by rising demand for refined zinc and a steady drawdown in stocks, he said.
Cominco estimates Western refined zinc demand will reach around 6.5 million tonnes this year and about 6.6 million tonnes in 1998.
Western refined zinc supply this year, however, is projected at about 6.3 million tonnes and seen inching up to around 6.4 million tonnes next year.
This would result in a supply gap of about 210,000 tonnes in 1997 and nearly 230,000 tonnes in 1998, Cominco said.
Combined with supply deficits in 1995 and 1996 totalling some 580,000 tonnes, zinc stocks will be drawn down "to a fine, critical level," Blyth said.
Cominco believes year-end stocks of zinc may plunge to around 400,000-450,000 tonnes in 1998 from as high as 1.64 million tonnes in 1994.

"We're now in a period where inventories are getting worked down and that is happenning during the first half of 1997. I think what you are going to see is a trend upward. Unfortunately, when the market starts feeling tight, that's when you get the potential for price spikes," Blyth said.
Long-term zinc contract premiums over LME cash metal prices are also likely to rise, especially when the supply crunch hits towards the end of this year, he said.
"I don't see any upward pressure on the premiums right now. The pressure will be felt more towards the end of the year as we start negotiating 1998 contracts," Blyth said.
Long-term contract premiums negotiated by Cominco this year for high-grade zinc averaged about $110 a tonne, down from the $120 level in 1996 due to ample supplies of the metal.
Blyth said the prospect of higher prices has prompted buyers, led by companies in the United States, to begin booking their supplies forward to protect against an escalation in their zinc costs.
The bullish outlook for zinc will probably persist over the next two years, Blyth said.
"As we go into 1999 and 2000, you've got Korean zinc coming on, Australia (coming on). A lot of people are talking about expansion," he said.
Asia will contribute an increasing chunk of Cominco's sales as demand for the metal in the roofing, siding and automobile battery industries in the region rises.
"The U.S. is always going to be number one because it's right in our backdoor," Blyth said. "(But) Asia is a very strong number two. We're looking to put 25 percent of our zinc in Asia."
